zones.description_hook: The keys were never the problem on this surface. It is the paper that never got a verdict, the same few sheets sliding from one end to the other for weeks.
description_body: This is the landing surface just inside your front door, the spot where your pockets empty out at the end of the day. In this reset we tip the whole thing onto the floor, keys, tray, and every stacked sheet, so you can see the real volume for the first time. Then we run all six passes on this one surface: Sort, Straighten, Shine, Safety the fourth S, Standardize, and Sustain.

The heart of it is the paper. Every sheet gets one of three answers, and only three: act, file, or recycle. Nothing comes back onto the surface undecided. The sheets that need you go upright into a folder with the date written in the corner, and that date becomes the clock that decides for you later. You will also see where the tray actually belongs, set by where your hand opens on the way in, and why the charger has to sit at the dry end, away from anything that drips off a wet sleeve.

Safety here is real and physical. Water and electricity meet under the hooks, one outlet quietly gets overloaded, and a bag on the floor is the thing you trip over in the dark with your arms full. We deal with all three while the surface is clear.

Done looks like this: the tray, the folder standing beside it, and nothing else. A small photo of that finished state taped inside the cupboard door so it teaches itself, and a habit tied to a moment you already have, the pause when you take your coat off. If your entryway keeps collecting paper it never resolves, this is the one surface to start with.
zones.pinned_comment: The rule that changed this surface for me: every sheet of paper gets one of three verdicts and only three, act, file, or recycle, and nothing goes back down undecided. The date in the folder corner does the rest. What is the paper that keeps sliding back and forth on your landing surface, the one that never quite gets a decision?

shorts.short_title: Lift the key tray and read the grey ring underneath #Shorts
shorts.caption: That grey film under your key tray is not really dirt, it is a record of how long since anyone cleaned here. You clean this surface to read it, not to impress. Wipe the surface first, then the tray. Full reset in the main episode.

shorts.caption: Three hazards come off one landing surface: water dripping onto the charger, an overloaded outlet, and a bag on the floor you trip over in the dark. Safety is the fourth S. One dock, one outlet, nothing else. Full reset in the main episode.

shorts.short_title: The 14-day folder rule that keeps entryway paper honest #Shorts
shorts.caption: The act folder empties after dinner, one sheet at a time, not in a batch. When a sheet passes fourteen days it stops being paperwork and becomes a decision: do it tonight or recycle it. Both are answers. Full reset in the main episode.

zones.description_hook: Somewhere on your coat rail is one good coat that cost real money and goes outside almost never. It survives every cull, while the coats you actually wear come down without a thought.
description_body: This is the coat rail just inside the front door, the one that fills up faster than any other spot in the house. In this episode you strip it bare, put back only the coats that earned their place through a full cold season of real outdoor use, and rebuild the whole zone around one idea. You count coats by weather, not by number. Each person gets one coat for each kind of weather your climate genuinely produces, and a second coat in the same category has to beat the first on a specific day you can name.

The rail matters because it is the first thing your hands reach for on the way out, and the first thing they drop on the way in. When it is overloaded, the coat you need is buried behind three you do not, and the floor below fills with bags nobody put away. The genuinely hard part here is that one expensive coat you almost never wear. Instead of giving it a guilty pass, you give it one honest trial on the front hook for two weeks, and let the answer settle itself.

You move through all six passes on this one rail: Sort, Straighten, Shine, Safety as the fourth pass, then Standardize and Sustain. Safety here is real and physical. A soaked winter coat is far heavier than the dry one you casually hang, so you hang your own weight on every hook, fit a proper wall anchor before one lets go, bring weight down low, and keep scarves and straps off the low hooks where a loop sits at a small child's neck height.

Finished looks like this. One coat per person for each kind of weather, wool on hangers and almost everything else on hooks, hats and gloves in one labeled bin you can read from the floor, umbrellas standing in the stand, and two hooks by the door left deliberately empty. Those two empty hooks are the whole standard. When every hook is full, one coat is in the wrong room, and the rail is quietly telling you to walk it back.
zones.pinned_comment: The idea that changed this zone for me is the two empty hooks by the door. They are not wasted space, they are a gauge. If the whole rail is full, one coat is in the wrong room and it is time to walk it back. Now the honest question: which coat is your one expensive coat that survives every cull but almost never goes outside? What is stopping you from giving it the two week trial on the front hook?

shorts.short_title: If a Coat Didn't Go Outdoors Last Winter, It Leaves #Shorts
shorts.caption: The coat you feel guiltiest about is usually the one that never goes outside. The test for what stays is simple, one full cold season of actual outdoor use. The full coat rail reset, all six passes, is in the episode.

shorts.short_title: Set Your Lowest Coat Hook by the Shortest Coat #Shorts
shorts.caption: Stop setting coat hooks at your own height. Hold the shortest person's own coat flat to the wall, mark the wall at its shoulder, and that becomes your lowest hook. The full entryway coat rail reset is in the episode.

shorts.short_title: There's Always Water in the Bottom of the Umbrella Stand #Shorts
shorts.caption: The umbrella stand is solid sided, so nobody ever looks inside, and there is always water and grit sitting in the bottom. Tip it out over a tray on the doorstep, do not wipe it. See the full coat rail reset in the episode.

shorts.short_title: A Soaked Winter Coat Is Heavier Than a Dry One, So Test Every Hook #Shorts
shorts.caption: A soaked winter coat is far heavier than the dry one you hang, and a hook in plain plasterboard pulls out later with a lump of wall behind it. Hang your full weight on each hook first, and fit the anchor now. Full reset in the episode.

shorts.short_title: Label the Bin So You Can Read It From the Floor #Shorts
shorts.caption: Write the contents and the season on the face of the shelf bin, then read it from the floor looking up, because that is exactly where you will be standing in October. If you can read it from down there, it works. Full coat rail reset in the episode.

shorts.short_title: Two Empty Hooks Tell You the Coat Rail Still Works #Shorts
shorts.caption: You put a wash on most days, so walk the rail on the way back and return any stray coat to a hook on that same trip. The two hooks by the door stay empty on purpose, and they are your gauge. Full reset in the episode.

zones.description_hook: You keep one pair for the mucky jobs, the tread worn smooth and the heel gone through on the outer edge. Turn that shoe sole up on the rack, and the sole settles what stays, not the memory attached to it.
description_body: In this reset we take on one shoe rack, the one just inside the front door that you never really empty. You pull every shoe out, pair them up in the open, and turn each pair sole up, because a rack is generous and lets an odd, worn shoe pass as half a pair. The sole decides what stays, not the memory attached to it. That is the first of six passes: Sort, Straighten, Shine, Safety, and then Standardize and Sustain.

This is the zone that decides how much grit reaches every other floor in the house. Wet soles on a hard floor are how people go down in a hallway. The grey salt crusted in the boot tray is exactly what scratches your wood and tile once a sole carries it back through the rooms. And the polish, suede cleaner, and waterproofing spray usually sit in an open basket at exactly the height a small child can reach. So this is not only tidying. It is a fall, a poison, and a crush handled while the rack is empty and easy to fix.

Done looks like this. Two pairs per person on the rack, soles down, at a height you reach standing up. Boots standing in the tray that catches the drip. A full stride of clear floor between the door and the rack, marked and kept empty. Every other pair lives somewhere that is not the entryway. Each shelf carries a name, so a third pair has visibly nowhere to stand and nobody has to police the count.

The habit that holds it is small and you can start it tonight. Shoes come off and go straight onto the rack before the coat comes off, while your hands are still free. And on the night the bins go out, the boot tray goes out with them and comes back empty. That is the whole standard, and it keeps itself.
zones.pinned_comment: The one idea from this episode: judge a shoe on its sole, not on the memory of what it cost or how it used to feel. A smooth tread, or a heel worn through on the outer edge, is no longer safe on a wet step, and that decision is already made before you pick it up. What is the one pair on your rack you keep for the mucky jobs but honestly never reach for? Turn it over tonight and tell me what the sole says.

shorts.short_title: Turn Every Shoe Over and Let the Sole Decide #Shorts
shorts.caption: The rack has been hiding this from you. Turn each pair sole up, and a smooth tread, or a heel worn through on its outer edge, tells you the shoe is no longer safe on a wet step. That is the whole test for what stays. The full six-step shoe and boot reset is in the main video.

shorts.short_title: The Boot Tray Grit That Scratches Your Floors #Shorts
shorts.caption: That grey crust in the bottom of the boot tray is not ordinary dirt. It is the salt and grit that scratches your hallway floor once a sole carries it back through the house. So you tip it and hose it, you never wipe it, and you do it when it looks dry, because dry is when it is at its worst. Full reset in the main video.

shorts.short_title: The Solvents at Toddler Height by Your Shoe Rack #Shorts
shorts.caption: The polish, the suede cleaner, and the waterproofing spray by the shoe rack are all solvents, and they usually sit in an open basket at exactly the height a small child can reach. Lift them onto a high shelf, or take them out of the room. Safety is the fourth of the six steps, and the full reset is in the main video.

shorts.short_title: Shoes Before Coat: The One Rule That Holds Your Shoe Rack #Shorts
shorts.caption: Shoes come off and go straight onto the rack before the coat comes off, while your hands are still free. Do it the other way and your hands fill up and the shoes stay wherever they landed. That one small order, shoes before coat, keeps the rack the way you left it. The full reset is in the main video.

zones.description_hook: You emptied this drawer a month ago, and here it is full again. The problem was never the clutter. It is that the drawer never had a job.
description_body: This is the bench just inside the front door, the one with a drawer under the seat. It fills up faster than anywhere else in the house for a plain reason. It is the nearest flat surface you reach on the way in, so anything you do not want to carry one more step lands here. The drawer is not failing you. It simply never had a single job, so it takes whatever you hand it.

In this reset you walk the bench through all six passes. Sort, where every item answers one question and only one. Straighten, where each section of the drawer gets a name so it stops accepting anything at all. Shine, where the drawer comes right out and the seat gets wiped, because people sit here in the same clothes they wore outside. Safety, the fourth S, where a tall narrow console gets strapped to the wall so it cannot tip forward onto a small child, and loose button batteries come out of the back corners. Standardize, where the rule for the bench top goes onto a small card taped inside the drawer. And Sustain, where the whole thing hangs on a movement you already make.

The question that does the real work is this. Would you need this while wearing your outdoor shoes, on the way out or in the first seconds back in. A screwdriver fails it. Birthday candles fail it. The case for a phone nobody owns fails it. None of them are rubbish. They just belong in another room.

Finished looks like three things on the bench top, a seat with nothing on it, and a drawer where every section holds one named category with the bare base showing between them. Keep that, and the drawer stops quietly turning back into the place things go to be forgotten.
zones.pinned_comment: The thing that keeps this drawer honest is not willpower, it is one question asked out loud: would you need this while wearing your outdoor shoes, on the way out or the first seconds back in. Everything else lives in another room. So tell me, what is the one item sitting in your entry drawer right now that you know would fail that test?

zones.description_hook: The mat just inside your door can look completely fine and have quietly stopped working. Once the fibres flatten and the grit rides on top of the pile, every shoe lifts it back off and carries it down the hall.
description_body: This is the last zone in the entryway, the door, the mat, and the strip of floor right inside it. It is the smallest patch in the house and it quietly does the most work, because everything that reaches the rest of your floors crosses it first. In this reset you clear the floor to one rule, set up the two mats that actually do the job, clean the one part of the mat everyone skips, deal with the trip waiting at the threshold, and give the mat a home anyone can see.

The test for a mat is simpler than the label on it. Walk across the inside mat at your normal pace and watch your feet. On most mats the second foot lands past the end, onto bare floor, and that is exactly how the grit gets past. Length is what matters here, not the pattern. A coarse mat outside scrapes, an absorbent mat inside dries, and both feet have to land on the inside one or it is too short to catch anything.

Safety is the fourth of the six passes, and it is never the one you skip. It deals with the curled corner you catch when your arms are full and your eyes are down, the mat that slides on hard floor even lying flat, and the loose door hinge that swings harder than you expect and catches a finger against the frame. Then you tape a thin outline on the floor, so the mat's home is something anyone can read at a glance instead of a rule that lives only in your head.

Finished looks like this. Two mats lying dead flat inside their taped outlines, not a curled corner on either one, nothing stored on the floor inside the swing of the door, and a door that latches on the first push. The standard that holds all of it is the simplest one in the house. Nothing is stored on this floor, ever. And the trigger is the last key of the night, when whoever comes home last straightens the mat with a foot before they turn it.
zones.pinned_comment: The thing that surprised me most making this: a mat can look completely fine and still have stopped working. Once the fibres flatten and the grit rides on top of the pile, it hands that grit straight to the next shoe instead of holding it. The real test is a stride, not a look. Both feet have to land on the inside mat, or it is too short to catch anything. So here is my question for you. What lands on the strip of floor just inside your front door that should not be there? For a lot of us it is the returns pile that never quite gets a home. Tell me what collects on yours.

shorts.caption: The strip of floor just inside your door is not storage. Everything on it comes up in a single pass tonight, and the returns pile that keeps drifting there gets a named spot in another room. The full door and mat reset is in the episode.

shorts.short_title: Why You Want Two Doormats, Not One #Shorts
shorts.caption: A coarse mat outside to scrape, an absorbent mat inside to dry. Two jobs, two mats. Then the real test: walk in at your normal pace and both feet have to land on the inside mat, or it is too short to stop the grit. Full reset in the episode.

shorts.short_title: The Grit Line Your Doormat Never Caught #Shorts
shorts.caption: Run a cloth along the threshold and you pull up a dark line of grit that was heading for the rest of your floors. Vacuum both faces of the mat, the underside too, then beat it outdoors. The full door and mat reset is in the episode.

shorts.short_title: The Curled Doormat Corner That Trips You #Shorts
shorts.caption: You step in with your arms full and your eyes down, and your toe finds the edge that lifted. Grip it flat, check the mat will not slide, and tighten the loose door hinge while you are down there. Safety is the fourth pass. Full reset in the episode.

shorts.short_title: The Tape Outline That Stops a Doormat Drifting #Shorts
shorts.caption: While the mat sits in the right spot, run a thin line of tape around it, then lift it and you have an outline on the floor. Now anyone can see the moment it wanders off square. The full door and mat reset is in the episode.
